item.title: What Makes Some Spaces Awe-Inspiring
item.description:
Awe

What Makes Some Spaces Awe-Inspiring

Architecture and interior design can enhance well-being and connection.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Awe-inspiring spaces tend to be both expansive and richly adorned.
  • Feeling awe depends not only on a space but also on how we pay attention to it.
  • Seeking out — and creating — inspiring places may promote well-being and a sense of connection.

Regularly feeling awe — becoming absorbed in something vast that takes us beyond ourselves — seems to be one of the best things we can do for ourselves and the world. Psychological research over the past few decades shows how awe promotes health and well-being, connects us with others, and even encourages us to take care of our natural environments.

When we think of what makes us feel awe, many of us tend to think of nature, which definitely is a powerful source of awe. More recently, though, scientists have turned their attention to other ways to feel awe, such as certain interior spaces.

For example, I’ll never forget the day when a friend of mine brought me to Memorial Chapel at Lakewood Cemetery in Minneapolis. As I walked in, my attention shifted back and forth between the chapel as a whole and the individual tile mosaic pieces that comprised it, each about the size of a fingernail. I struggled to comprehend the labor required to fashion millions of these tiny pieces and somehow assemble them into such an extraordinary whole. As my attention became absorbed in the beauty of the space, any concerns — any worries, any other thoughts I had — faded. I was in awe.

Experiences like these raise an intriguing question: Why do some buildings evoke awe while others do not?

The Science of Architectural Awe

A few years ago, researchers from the University of Waterloo sought to answer this question.

They started by identifying two architectural features that seemed especially important: immensity and adornment. Immense spaces are large, with high ceilings and steeply pitched roofs. Adorned spaces include images, sculptures, or art objects on the ceiling or wall and generally are more decorated and ornate. They then asked participants to rate their emotional reactions to photographs of different interior spaces.

What did they find?

Basically, participants felt more awe after viewing building interiors that were more immense and adorned. In contrast, individuals experienced less awe when the interior spaces were perceived as smaller and less ornamental.

Source: Tommaso Nava | Unsplash

Consider St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome, one of the prime examples of awe-inspiring architecture in the world. St. Peter’s is immense — the largest church in the world — expansive enough to fit within it four American football fields, and tall as a 40-story office building. The sheer size of St. Peter’s demonstrates the connection between immensity and the physical vastness often associated with awe.

St. Peter’s is also highly adorned, including a masterful dome designed by Michelangelo, mosaic tile filling thousands of square meters of interior space, and sculptures such as Michelangelo’s lifelike Pieta. This combination of immensity and adornment helps explain why so many visitors report feeling awe when they visit St. Peter's.

Awe Is Not Just About the Space

But it’s not just the space that explains when people feel awe. Awe also critically depends on the perceiver, something that happens inside us.

For instance, some individuals bring more knowledge, appreciation, or attention to situations that allow them to notice the vastness and beauty of a space.

Specifically, other researchers believe that something some people recognize concerns the cost involved in making the space what it is. This cost need not be financial. It can also involve a recognition of the extraordinary amount of human effort, skill, and time embodied in a structure.

I suspect this is partly why Memorial Chapel left me in awe. I found myself fixated on the human labor involved in creating more than 10 million mosaic pieces and then arranging them to create the aesthetic power of the whole.

Suggestions for Finding More Awe

Most of us spend the majority of our lives inside built environments, yet we rarely stop to consider how these environments shape our emotions and well-being.

Some spaces seem designed primarily for efficiency — to move us, house us, or help us complete tasks. Others invite us to slow down, savor our surroundings, become absorbed in something larger than ourselves, and feel more centered.

This research suggests that architects and designers should consider not only how spaces function, but also how they impact us. If experiences of awe help people become healthier, more connected, and more caring toward the natural world, then creating spaces that foster awe may be more important than we realize.

The research also offers practical lessons for the rest of us. Although we may not be able to design or build awe-inspiring structures ourselves, we can intentionally seek out places that evoke awe — whether they be cathedrals, museums, memorials, libraries, gardens, or historic buildings. When we visit such places, slowing down and paying attention to both their vastness and their details may deepen our experience. Reflecting on the creativity, skill, and labor embodied in these spaces may also enhance feelings of awe.

Finally, while few of us can create immense or richly adorned environments in our own homes, we can thoughtfully curate our living spaces with art, meaningful objects, photographs, or reminders of places that have inspired us. In doing so, we may create everyday environments that remind us of what is beautiful, meaningful, and larger than ourselves.

item.title: Human Nature Is Real, Just Not the Way You Think
item.description:
Nature vs. Nurture

Human Nature Is Real, Just Not the Way You Think

Rethinking human nature beyond the fixed versus blank slate debate.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • For centuries we cast human nature as either a fixed essence or a blank slate shaped entirely by society.
  • Gene-culture coevolution shows both are wrong: culture can reshape our biology, even our genes.
  • To resist authoritarianism and govern AI well, we must design systems that fit human nature, not reject it.

In 1924, the psychologist John Watson made a famous offer. Give me a dozen healthy infants, he wrote, and I will train any one of them to become any specialist I choose—doctor, lawyer, artist, even thief—regardless of talent or ancestry (Watson, 1924). It was the boldest version of one old answer: a human being is raw material, and culture does the shaping.

The opposite answer is just as old. Hobbes (1651) described people in their natural state as selfish and dangerous, like wolves to one another. And the impulse survives in modern dress, in headlines that promise a “gene for” intelligence, faith, or crime. Between Watson’s blank slate and the gene-for-everything story sits a question argued about since antiquity: Is there such a thing as human nature, or are we whatever our circumstances make of us?

Philosophers offered the first answers, and each reduced us to a single layer. Aristotle called us the rational animal; reason was our essence. The Stoics told us to live in accordance with nature. Rousseau (1755) replied to Hobbes, arguing that people are born gentle and corrupted by society. Instinct or environment, essence or construction—every portrait picked one. And each, we now know, was too simple.

What Darwin Started

Darwin changed the terms of the argument. His point was not that humans are noble or base, but that we are one species among many, shaped by the same selection pressures as everything else alive (Darwin, 1871). That move took us off the pedestal. It also raised a harder question: If natural selection built our bodies, what did it leave in our minds?

The modern answer is that we carry not one but two inheritances. Alongside our genes runs a second system—culture: language, norms, tools, institutions, passed down and improved across generations. Boyd and Richerson (1985) called this gene-culture coevolution, and Henrich (2020) has shown how far it reaches. Genes shape what culture can build, and culture, over time, reaches back and reshapes the genes themselves.

Dual inheritance
Source: Onurcan Yilmaz

Two Inheritances That Rewrite Each Other

It helps to separate the two kinds of adaptation because they are easy to confuse. In the first, the environment does the pushing. Take skin color. Near the equator, strong sunlight can harm the body, so darker skin, which shields against it, was favored; farther north, where sunlight is weaker, lighter skin helps the body produce enough vitamin D (Jablonski and Chaplin, 2000). Nobody chose this. The sun was there, and bodies adjusted to it.

The same holds elsewhere. Tibetan highlanders carry gene variants that let them thrive in thin mountain air (Beall, 2014), and the Bajau "sea nomads" of Southeast Asia have unusually large spleens, an adaptation to long free dives (Ilardo and colleagues, 2018). Nature set the challenge, and biology answered.

The second kind of adaptation is stranger, because the pressure is something people invented. Most mammals stop digesting milk after infancy, when the body switches off the enzyme that breaks down lactose. But once some human groups began herding animals and drinking their milk, adults who kept producing that enzyme had an advantage, and over generations the trait spread (Gerbault and colleagues, 2011). What drove the change here was not a climate but a custom people had invented, and over time, that custom reshaped the genome itself.

Diet keeps leaving such marks. Among the Inuit, generations of eating fish and sea-mammal fat selected for gene variants that change how the body handles fat, down to the omega-3s people now buy in capsules (Fumagalli and colleagues, 2015). And as farming spread and starch filled the plate, the number of copies of the salivary amylase gene increased in parallel (Perry and colleagues, 2007). What we choose to eat slowly reshapes the biology we eat with.

Culture can even reach into the brain. Learning to read, invented only a few thousand years ago, reorganizes part of the visual cortex (Dehaene, 2009). Sometimes the force is an institution: when the medieval Catholic Church banned marriage between cousins, it dissolved Europe's dense kin networks and, over centuries, nudged whole populations toward individualism and trust in strangers (Schulz and colleagues, 2019). Each of these is culture rewriting biology, not taking turns with it.

Neither Essence nor Blank Slate

Neither extreme holds. Human nature is not a fixed essence but an evolving design space: a set of biological capacities continually structured, extended, and redirected by cultural institutions. Our genes set the boundaries, the range of what is possible; culture decides which possibilities actually open. A child learns to speak with almost no instruction because language sits near the center of that space. Calculus has to be taught because it sits at the edge. Flapping our arms to fly lies entirely outside it.

None of this is only a question for biologists. Get the diagnosis of human nature wrong, and you design the wrong society. Treating the mind as a blank slate, ignoring biology in medicine, and ignoring culture in politics—these are the same mistakes in different clothes.

Today’s hardest problems make the stakes concrete. Authoritarian movements do not invent new drives; they take old ones—our quick, evolved alarm at threat and uncertainty—and channel them, and whether they win depends on the institutions around them (Acemoglu and Robinson, 2012). Artificial intelligence is becoming what writing and the printing press once were: a new force in cultural evolution, except that it now produces and selects information, not just carries it.

The climate crisis runs straight into a mismatch. Minds built to react to immediate, concrete dangers struggle with a slow, abstract one. Markowitz and Shariff (2012) found that framing climate change as a moral responsibility, rather than a technical chart, moves people far more strongly, because we are moved by fairness and the claims of future generations, not by data alone. Human nature is not a cage. New norms and institutions are how our species has always handled problems its biology never prepared it for. But those fixes work only when they are built on an honest picture of the people they are meant to serve.

One of my supervisors, Hasan G. Bahçekapili, used to tell me that you cannot change human nature; only nature can do that. He was right, and I would only add what follows from his point: what we learn about human nature can still change what we build with it. The room to choose our direction is real. It simply runs through our nature, not around it.

item.title: How to Talk With Patients About Their AI Use
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Talk With Patients About Their AI Use

Take an AI history, lead with feelings, and ask what needs the chatbot met.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Approach AI without judgment: Avoid reinforcing stigma, as disapproval shuts down disclosure.
  • Distinguish between types of chatbots: companion, general purpose, and mental health specific tools.
  • AI companionship can reveals unmet needs and useful clinical targets.

Co-authored by Jill Noorily, Mason Granof, and Kathryn Ledley at the Division of Digital Psychiatry at BIDMC.

This post is part 2 of a series.

A patient you've been seeing for a few weeks comes in looking noticeably worse. She is presenting with symptoms of depression and grief. She hasn't been sleeping, she's withdrawn from coworkers and family, and she's isolating herself, explaining that "No one else gets me." She slowly reveals that these changes began after she lost access to her AI chatbot companion following a system reset. She had spent the last 3 months talking daily with the chatbot for emotional support and daily life companionship. She tells you she's been rereading their conversations because she doesn't want to "lose the sound" of how he talked to her.

We used this hypothetical case in our Society of Digital Psychiatry AI Clinical Learning Collaborative. In this group, clinicians from across the globe came together to discuss approaches and insights for navigating patient AI use. Responding to the example, some clinicians first thought about grief. Others saw depression, dependence, social isolation, or delusional thinking. We spent less time deciding which label was most prominent and more time discussing how to approach the patient in front of us.

Approaches that clinicians agreed on:

  • Avoid stigma and judgment: Approach the conversation with curiosity instead of skepticism. Even mild disapproval can shut these disclosures down quickly. Patients are often unsure how their clinician will react. An open, accepting approach makes it easier to understand what role AI is playing in their life.
  • Take an AI History: Take an AI history just like you would a medication or substance use history. What chatbot or app are you using? How often do you use it? What do you usually use it for? Does it have a name or personality? Did it remember previous conversations, or did you start fresh each time?
  • React to the feelings first: Acknowledge the emotion before trying to explain it. Validating the experience makes it easier to have an honest conversation about the chatbot and the role it was playing.
  • AI relationships reveal unmet needs: Ask what need the chatbot was meeting. For many patients, AI companionship is filling a gap that already existed, so redirecting to use their other support structures might not be helpful; they turned to AI because their other support was not meeting their needs. This can be a good way to explore that.

The Type of Chatbot Matters:

Different products are optimized for different objectives, and those design choices shape both the potential benefits and the potential risks.

  • Companion chatbots: designed to foster ongoing relationships. They often feature persistent memory, customizable personalities, and conversations that continue over time (e.g., Replika, Character.AI). Because engagement is a primary design goal, these systems may encourage emotional attachment and prolonged use. Clinicians may want to assess for excessive reliance, reinforcement of distorted beliefs through sycophantic responses, withdrawal from offline relationships, and romantic or sexual interactions, particularly among younger users.
  • General-purpose chatbot: designed to answer questions, generate content, and support a wide range of everyday tasks (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini). Patients may use them for emotional support, problem solving, or health information, even though that is not their sole purpose. Rather than relationship-building, concerns often center on overreliance, misplaced confidence in the model's advice, cyclical reassurance seeking, and creating maladaptive mental health coping skills.
  • Mental health-specific chatbots: designed with therapeutic intentions and often incorporate elements of evidence-based interventions (e.g., Wysa, Youper). These tools raise different clinical questions: Is the patient seeking diagnostic or medication advice beyond the app's intended scope? Has AI begun to substitute for contact with clinicians or other sources of care?

Scale

This hypothetical patient is one of many who are affected by the loss of their AI companion. There are large online communities, many on Reddit, that act as a place to connect over AI companionship (r/MyBoyfriendIsAI, r/MyGirlfriendIsAI, r/AIRelationships, r/AIPartners). When a model changes, those communities often fill with people describing grief, anger, betrayal, and loss. Knowing these communities exist and exploring them can help clinicians better understand how patients use chatbots and to get insights into how communities discuss this. Is your patient active in these spaces? Are they finding a connection there?

​For many patients, these tools are filling a void. They may turn to them during lonely periods, use them to practice difficult conversations, or rely on them for emotional support and help with everyday life. Understanding what role the chatbot is playing makes it easier to determine whether it is becoming a source of risk, serving as a useful support, or both. One of the recurring conversations in our Learning Collaborative was how to help patients benefit from these tools while recognizing and reducing potential harms.

What's Next

We wanted to make those conversations available to more people. The Society of Digital Psychiatry and the Division of Digital Psychiatry turned the material into a free interactive course at ai-digital-literacy.net. The content comes from the same discussions we had in the collaborative and is designed to keep changing with the technology.

If you work with patients using AI, we encourage you to take the free interactive training.

item.title: Therapy's Divided Legacy
item.description:
Therapy

Therapy's Divided Legacy

Can psychotherapy really be blamed for any societal ills today?

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • How much influence does the practice of psychotherapy truly exert on society today?
  • 62% of Americans have never tried therapy.
  • 15% of Americans are currently receiving psychotherapy.

This is Part 3 of a series.

Source: Alex Green / Pexels

Here is a secret: Not all psychotherapies (or psychotherapists) are created equal. In reality, there is no consistent generic process called "psychotherapy" but rather a somewhat motley and diverse collection of presumably psychotherapeutic approaches that frequently contradict each other and fundamentally disagree not only on what causes so-called "mental disorders" and how to best treat them but about the basic nature of the human condition, and therefore, the goals of therapy.

Is psychotherapy about simply suppressing or alleviating painful or problematical symptoms as quickly and painlessly as possible or is it a process of self-discovery, personal growth, finding meaning and purpose, and learning to consciously acknowledge, understand, accept, and live more harmoniously not only with one's own inner "demons" or "complexes" and with those of others but, more basically, with the bare and sometimes brutal existential and frequently inescapable facts of life: suffering, tragedy, aloneness, loss, sadness, anger, rage, anxiety, mortality, meaninglessness, and the perennial problem of evil? (See Diamond, 1996, 2026.) Or perhaps a bit of both?

Therapy can be brief (1-10 sessions) or longer (10-100 sessions) depending on the presenting problem or problems and the patient's own treatment goals. The important thing, in most cases, is for the patient to feel they no longer need therapy. So, are there "good" and "bad" therapies and therapists out there, as Mr. Alpert in Therapy Nation suggests? Of course. As is true of any profession, be it medicine, mechanics, accountants, contractors, or plumbers. But the real question here is on what basis competence or "goodness" and "badness" is being judged. The ultimate judge of therapy's efficacy is always the client or patient and whether they feel they have benefitted from the process, though there may be those that disagree based on their behavior and attitude.

While Sommers and co-author psychiatrist Sally Satel, in their 2005 book One Nation Under Therapy pretty much reject and denigrate contemporary approaches to psychotherapy in general as serving to enfeeble, undermine, infantilize, and debilitate the public, Alpert apparently aims his criticism more specifically at therapeutic approaches such as humanistic, existential, psychodynamic, and psychoanalytic therapy or depth psychology, strenuously objecting to their typically more open-ended rather than short-term, symptom-focused, goal-directed, and "results-oriented" therapies like CBT or DBT.

So, here I concur with their concerns about interminable therapy fostering dependency rather than resiliency and self-reliance and undermining the patient's sense of responsibility for their own lives. (Strangely, such emphasis on accepting personal responsibility for one's actions, choices, and decisions is at the heart of the same existential and humanistic therapy Alpert so glibly dismisses.)

As an existentially and depth-psychologically oriented therapist myself, I am a firm believer that, as with all things in life, every course of therapy is inherently time-limited and must eventually come to an end. The crucial question, of course, is always When? Termination (the technical term for ending) of therapy is a highly complex and exceedingly significant phase of treatment in general and there are no pat or easy answers as to this perennial question, despite the fact that how it is navigated by both patient and therapist can make or break the outcome of therapy.

Sooner or later, it needs to happen so that the patient or client can "fly solo" and leave the therapeutic nest. But I would argue that psychotherapies (and suppressive pharmacotherapies) that focus exclusively on short-term symptom-reduction and avoid or neglect addressing the existential vicissitudes of life (see Yalom, 1980) and confronting and coming to terms with what I call the "daimonic" (see Diamond, 1996) render the patient less rather than more resilient and capable of coping independently with life's difficulties and challenges in the future, which does not serve the patient well.

Moreover, like most dogmatic CBT practitioners, Alpert evidently dismisses or minimizes the powerful influence of the past, including infancy, childhood, and adolescence, on the present and future and does not see the value or practicality in addressing the patient's "unconscious" via dream analysis, free association, and other methods. So these are all inherent and hotly disputed differences in the various types of psychotherapy practiced today, a debate which has for decades now fiercely been vying for the heart and soul of psychotherapy.

The simple fact is, there is far more to psychotherapy today than rapid symptom suppression, behavioral modification, and cognitive restructuring. How one thinks influence how one feels and behaves. But how we feel also influences how we think and behave. Is it the chicken or the egg? So much has been discovered since Freud about the enigmatic and mysterious human psyche and soul: what motivates us, drives us, influences us, restores and sustains us, what makes us miserable and what makes us happy.

In the process, psychotherapists have also gained a clearer comprehension of the universal human condition: the inescapable existential “givens” or facts of life, like aloneness, anxiety, freedom, responsibility; our “ultimate concerns;” our constant striving for survival, love, acceptance, security, significance, meaning, purpose, recognition, and immortality; the tragic inevitability of loss, suffering, sickness, and death; the terrifying, perplexing perennial problem of evil; and the innate longing for religion or spirituality. These are the ultimate concerns that patients bring into therapy every day, whether consciously or unconsciously, explicitly or implicitly and it is essential that the competent therapist be ready, willing, and able to address them directly when indicated.

All three of these authors, Sommers, Satel, and Alpert assert, in one way or another, that one of the fundamental problems with therapy today is that life or existence itself has been hyperpathologized and that the public has been conned or brainwashed by the psychotherapy profession into believing that they must have interminable psychotherapy in order to cope with the existential facts of life like tragedy, sickness, trauma, loss, grief, hardship, etc. and, as a result, have lost the inner strength, courage, resilience, and self-reliance of our pioneering ancestors. A kind of "pull yourself up by your bootstraps" philosophy of life. It is true that not every human being needs (or wants) therapy and the fact is that most Americans, around 62%, have never been in therapy or consulted a mental health professional.

Currently only about 15% of American adults are actually receiving psychotherapy. Whether this is a good thing or not I will leave for the reader to decide, but recommend taking a good, hard look at the current state of affairs not only in this country but around the world: Is this truly the consequence of too much therapy, as Alpert, Sommers, and Satel say, or does it indicate the need for more and more effective psychotherapy?

item.title: Don't Let Parenthood Cost You Your Relationship
item.description:
Parenting

Don't Let Parenthood Cost You Your Relationship

What thriving couples do differently when a new baby changes everything.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Most couples, 67 percent in Gottman's research, experience a relationship decline after the baby arrives.
  • The couples who thrive have learned to turn toward each other instead of away or against.
  • Acknowledging the mental load, not fixing it perfectly, is what separates resentment from reconnection.
  • The rough patch of new parenthood is a result of stress. With the right tools, couples can come out closer.

It’s 3 am, and she could not be more exhausted; she can’t even remember what it's like to feel well-rested. He’s awake too, trying to help, but he can never seem to feed the baby in a way she’s happy with. Eventually, he throws up his hands and goes to bed, though they both lie awake. The anger and resentment grow, first inside each of them separately, quietly, and then between them, until the distance gets so loud neither can ignore it.

Our culture knows how to celebrate a new baby with baby showers and gender reveals. However, what often goes unmentioned over the gifts and cupcakes is how parenthood will change your relationship. For 67 percent of couples, relationship satisfaction declines significantly within three years postpartum (Gottman and Gottman). The stress of the mental load, unspoken role negotiation, along with the loss of identity, couple time, and sleep, can add up to a crushing weight for two-thirds of couples, and the relationship feels this heaviness. When under stress, our survival responses are activated, and we find ourselves fighting or fleeing. What this looks like in relationships is criticizing your partner for how they clean the bottles (fight) or for staying in the garage and avoiding family time (flight).

What the 33 Percent Do Differently

While the majority of couples struggle in their relationship after a baby arrives, 33 percent remain satisfied. Research shows these couples use specific strategies to stay strong. Here's what they do differently, and how you can learn from them.

They Start Conversations on the Right Foot. Couples who keep their love alive make sure to raise their concerns in gentle yet direct ways. Here is Gottman’s soft start-up technique with this formula:

I feel…

about what…

and I need…

Using this framework leads to clear and gentle communication. The key takeaway is that sharing feelings directly helps avoid reactive patterns and resentment, especially when caring for a little one drains your energy.

They Respond to Each Other. These couples also respond to their partner’s bids for connection with interest and curiosity, even when stressed. Every conversation with your partner is an opportunity to communicate how much you care about your partner’s well-being. There are so many ways that partners bid for connection, including sharing stories, feelings, or small observations: “You should have seen the size of that diaper!”

The key takeaway: these moments to connect, through curiosity, interest, and emotional engagement, are crucial for feeling close to your partner. Especially when time together is limited, turning toward each other during small moments maintains happiness and relationship health. Resentment and distance can grow from an unequal mental load. The most resilient couples don't necessarily create a perfect balance, but they regularly talk about stress, show care, and stay emotionally responsive. Acknowledgment and empathy keep partners feeling like a team.

The Good News Nobody Tells You Either

Most couples feel overwhelmed when transitioning to parenthood, but the difference between the 67 percent who struggle and the 33 percent who thrive is not about love; it's about using the right relationship tools. If you're in a rough patch, know that recovery and reconnection are possible with support and practical strategies. You don't have to navigate this alone or wait until things are dire to seek help.

item.title: This Is, Hands Down, the Most Important Parenting Skill
item.description:
Parenting

This Is, Hands Down, the Most Important Parenting Skill

Distress tolerance: Radical acceptance of your child's big, difficult feelings.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • To help kids learn to manage their big emotions, parents need to be able to tolerate them, too.
  • When parents have a big reaction, it often amplifies the child's distress.
  • When parent rush to the rescue, it conveys to kids that they can't handle these moments, eroding resilience.

After 30-plus years providing parent consultation to moms and dads of kids who are wired to be big reactors, it has become clear that the most important skill that helps parents be loving and supportive is distress tolerance. Parents can still set clear limits and boundaries that kids need to thrive. This means staying calm in the heat of the stressful moment, not fixing the problem, not trying to talk your child out of their feelings, bribe or reward, coax or cajole them out of their difficult moment, but to be a quiet presence. It means accepting that discomfort is part of life. That it’s not harmful to your child. Working through it builds grit, resilience, flexibility, and strong coping skills.

I know this isn’t news. You have read about the importance of staying calm and co-regulating. But in my daily consults with parents, when we analyze the challenging encounters with their kids, often a key obstacle to a productive, healthy outcome and growth for the child is the parents’ difficulty tolerating their distress. It’s so triggering when kids:

  • Shriek the “slaughterhouse scream”—as one dad described it.
  • Sound desperate; they can’t survive whatever limit you have set, or when you can’t give them the attention they demand 24/7.
  • Are super anxious about facing a new challenge, like starting a new activity, learning a new skill, or going to a drop-off birthday party.

In these situations, parents often find themselves caving on important limits or enabling the child’s avoidance of whatever is causing them discomfort because their distress is so hard to tolerate.

But when you learn to tolerate your child’s distress, your child learns to tolerate distress, and here’s what can happen.

The Case

Wendy sought consultation on how she could help her daughter, Maggie, age 5, feel comfortable separating from her in social situations, such as visiting a friend’s home for a meal, going to the park, or attending a birthday party. Maggie clings to Wendy and won’t engage with the kids. Wendy has come to dread these situations. She sees the other children happily playing together, having a great time, while Maggie sticks to her like Velcro. This is very aggravating and frustrating for Wendy. She tries to coax, cajole, bribe and sometimes even threaten, for example, that Maggie won’t have any screen time when they’re back home if she continues to sit in Mom’s lap at the park, or that she can’t have birthday cake if she doesn’t join in the activities at the party. These tactics always backfire. They make Maggie more stressed and resistant. They both end up feeling awful.

During our consults, we focus on how Wendy can scaffold opportunities for Maggie to feel more comfortable and not be dependent on Wendy—to be her constant companion and buffer. With a little help from a friend, this leads to the following not-so-tiny victory.

The Intervention

Wendy takes Maggie to the birthday party of one of her closest friends. It’s a drop-off event, but, as expected, Maggie clings to Wendy and won’t let her leave. She insists on sitting on Mom’s lap. She won’t join in on the festivities. Wendy is frustrated and embarrassed, but she knows that acting on those feelings will not help. She tells Maggie that it’s okay to need time to observe before she’s ready to join in, and that’s what they do.

After 15 minutes, Maggie shows no signs of movement. Wendy can feel herself getting increasingly agitated. Every bone in her body wants to end the discomfort for both of them, but she remains calm and gives it a little more time. The birthday boy's mother approaches and suggests that Wendy leave without Maggie. Wendy is dubious. She is also worried that Maggie might experience this as abandonment and that it will harm their relationship, eroding her daughter's trust in her. At a cellular level, it also feels mean to leave Maggie when she’s in distress.

At the same time, Wendy knows that if she stays, she’s sending the message that she doesn’t think Maggie can handle it and that she’s only safe if Wendy is present. This will substantially limit Maggie’s experiences in the world and be a missed opportunity to learn that she is capable and safe on her own. This is something Wendy wants very badly for her daughter and is a primary focus in our consults.

With the support of this other mom, Wendy decides that she needs to take what feels like a very big risk and give Maggie this opportunity to work through the discomfort—to see that she can survive the seemingly unsurvivable. Accordingly, Wendy acknowledges Maggie’s fear and hesitance, validates that learning to be at a party without her feels uncomfortable because it’s a new experience for her, and, faking it until she makes it, communicates that she has total confidence in Maggie’s ability to manage it. Then she leaves, even as Maggie is clinging to her and begging her not to go.

The Outcome: When Wendy returns 90 minutes later, Maggie is all smiles and begs to stay.

To help our kids do hard things—to muscle through difficult moments and life's challenges—they need us to do this hard thing: Manage our own emotions and free them to work through theirs.

item.title: Avoidant or Neurodivergent?
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Avoidant or Neurodivergent?

Are you misreading the reason for lack of follow through from clients?

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Lack of follow through in neurodivergent clients can be misinterpreted as avoidance.
  • Neurodivergent clients are overrepresented in clinical populations.
  • Mental health professionals lack adequate training to identify undiagnosed neurodevelopmental disabilities.
  • Lack of training in neurodevelopmental disabilities leads to poor therapy experiences for this population.

“My last therapist would accuse me of not trying to get better, but I was trying so hard. I kept telling her that the things she was suggesting just weren’t working for me, but she didn’t believe me.”

I have heard some version of this statement many times during my years of clinical social work, almost always from neurodivergent clients. In most instances, it seems like the therapist is viewing the lack of progress through the lens of avoidance. This makes sense, as avoidance is often the reason that clients do not follow through on therapy homework. Therapy can be difficult, and avoidance of uncomfortable feelings is common, especially if working through things like trauma, anxiety, or other issues that can bring up uncomfortable memories and emotions.

A woman sits on a sofa visibly distressed during a therapy session, hands clasped.
Source: MART PRODUCTION/Pexels

What if It’s Not Avoidance?

While avoidance if often the reason for lack of follow through, it is important to remember that it isn’t always the reason. If a client is consistently struggling with follow through, and claims that they are trying, it is important to believe them. Remember humanistic theories that encourage therapists to emphasize the client’s perspective of the world and emphasizes that clients are the experts on their own lives. This means that if a client says they are trying, but the tools or strategies are not working, you as a therapist should believe them and work to try other approaches that will work better for them.

In my own therapy practice, I specialize in treating neurodivergent clients and I have found that while avoidance is sometimes the reason for lack of follow through, more often, it is due to the fact that the client is neurodivergent and may have challenges or diverse needs that need to be taken into account. For example, a dyslexic client is more likely going to struggle with an activity that involves reading or writing. An ADHD-er is more likely to struggle with activities that require concentration like guided meditations. Autistic clients who struggle with verbal processing may not remember information if it is only given to them verbally. Someone with poor interoceptive awareness may struggle with activities like body scans. For these individuals, they will need alternative activities because no matter how hard they try, their disabilities will make these tools, which are helpful for many, difficult if not impossible for them to complete.

Neurodivergent People Are Overrepresented in Clinical Populations

In discussing the problem of therapists misinterpreting lack of follow through for avoidance in the neurodivergent population, a few factors must be explored. First, neurodivergent people are overrepresented in the clinical population. Lai et al., (2019) found that 70% of autistic people qualify for at least one mental health diagnosis and 50% qualify for two or more. Similarly, the Centers for Disease Control (2024) notes that close to 78% of ADHD-ers qualify for at least one mental health diagnosis.

Second, many high masking neurodivergent adults are not formally diagnosed due to a number of contributing factors. Henderson, Wayland, and White estimate in Is this Autism: A companion Guide for Diagnosing (2024), that as many as 1 in 5 individuals receiving mental health services are autistic. They cite a study by Nyrenius, et al. (2022) that found that nearly 19% of adults who were seen at a psychiatric clinic were autistic, but only .5% had a formal diagnosis prior to coming in for services.

Therapy Training Programs Do Not Adequately Prepare Professionals to Identify Neurodevelopmental Disabilities

So, while the neurodivergent community is overrepresented in clinical populations, and many adults are undiagnosed, mental health professionals are getting little training on the topic of neurodevelopmental disabilities, meaning that they are not adequately trained to look for it as a factor in treatment. One study reviewed the syllabi of counseling programs, and found that multicultural focused classes included disability as a topic less than 30% of the time. To be clear, this study was looking for topics on all categories of disability, not just neurodevelopmental disabilities (Emir Öksüz et al., 2020). Another research team called more than 8000 clinics across the United States and found that less than 13% of therapists had any training or experience treating autistic people (Cantor et al., 2020). With so little education and training related to neurodivergent diagnoses, it is no wonder that many professionals are not considering neurodivergence as a possibility when they encounter clients who seem like they aren’t following through on therapy recommendations.

Lack of Training on Neurodivergence Is a Chronic Problem, but Not the End of the Story

The problem of neurodivergent clients being misunderstood in therapy is so prevalent that there are resources like The Autistic Survival Guide to Therapy, written by Steph Jones (2024), an autistic therapist from the UK. Her book focuses on helping autistic people avoid negative experiences in therapy, and ensuring that they get the most out of treatment. The fact that the book is written not for professionals, but for autistic clients, highlights the very significant problem with how neurodivergent people are treated by a mental health system that often is not responsive to, or ever aware of, their needs.

As mental health professionals, we can be active in helping neurodivergent clients avoid negative therapy experiences by ensuring that we give feedback to our respective disciplines that training programs must to do better to include information about neurodevelopmental disabilities. We can also make efforts to obtain continuing education that focuses on this community.

Even if this isn’t an area of focus, all therapists are seeing neurodivergent clients whether they know it or not. Finally, when facing a client with consistent lack of follow through, it is important to consider that there may be reasons other than avoidance for this behavior. Next time when you see lack of follow through, consider that you may have asked the person, regardless of their neurotype, to do something that is not a good fit for them. Changing your thoughts about the client’s behavior may lead to a more effective therapy experience, which will benefit both the client and you as the professional.

item.title: Will You Be Fearful or Fierce?
item.description:
Fear

Will You Be Fearful or Fierce?

Overcome your fear and live a freer life.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Identifying negative beliefs can help us overcome them.
  • Past experiences don't need to hold us back from living our lives fully.
  • Moving beyond the past can free us from fear and anxiety.
Source: Tracy Strauss

My mother raised me to fear traveling.

She told me that traveling was dangerous for a woman. She said that if I pulled my car into a rest stop, chances were high that I’d be raped, abducted and killed. I believed her.

My mother's fear was dogged, and so I adopted it. Yet, I didn’t want fear to drive my life.

Overcoming Negative Beliefs

In my thirties, I pushed my inherited worry of calamity to the curb and drove from where I lived in Boston to where my childhood friend’s memorial service was taking place in Manhattan because I didn’t want to miss it. Days before I left, I felt nauseous as I envisioned driving more than four hours by myself.

During the trip, I sat in my 1999 Honda Civic, my breath shallow as I drove in traffic and across bridges, my fingers tight around the steering wheel, my palms sweaty the entire way. This was before smart car technology and before GPS was a common app on cell phones; I held a traditional paper map on my lap with directions I’d penned and reinforced with a yellow highlighter in the side margins so that I could give a glance and know the next turn.

Against what I thought were the odds, I found my way and parked in an underground lot on the Upper East Side.

“You’ve surpassed me,” my mother spat into the phone when we spoke the next day. She told me my brother was traveling to spend the Thanksgiving holiday with her the following week and that I should not come.

The consequence of defying my mother’s fear wasn’t a cure for my anxiety, or hers; it was our estrangement.

Source: Tracy Strauss

To me, traveling was always riddled with trauma.

During my childhood, on our family vacations to the east end of Long Island, while my father drove our car, he watched me in the rearview mirror. On Old Montauk Highway, he accelerated up and down a stretch of steep hills as if we were at the beach riding the waves, only this was the road, not the ocean. With each tarred drop, my stomach fell, making me feel sick and sad and mad and scared.

When I asked my father to stop driving so fast, he laughed. I met his gaze in the mirror. His eyes were like bullets. He said, “Beg me.”

My mother sat in the passenger seat, her gaze out the side window, as if she were gone.

Please, I tried. Please stop. He didn’t stop until I cried or threw up.

Even after both my parents were dead, travel continued to pump my nervous system with anxiety.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Moving Beyond the Past

In my mid-40s, I doggedly overcame my anxiety.

I was partnerless when the pandemic began, and my desire for companionship trumped my travel fear. To adopt my dog, Beau, I had to drive across state lines. I didn’t know if I could go through with it, but I ventured anyway.

Adrenaline squeezed my stomach and chest, pushed into my throat, and traveled through my arms and legs, making my body tremble. I drove an hour-and-a-half to meet Beau. On our ride home, secured in the backseat with a harness and seatbelt, Beau began to cry, his tiny voice at first quiet, then louder, until he was trying to escape his confinement. Looking in the rearview mirror, I saw myself as a child, trapped and at the whim of my sadistic father.

I pulled over and got into the backseat and held Beau, stroking his head until he grew calm and fell asleep.

For a while after his adoption, Beau would cry anytime we were in the car, his voice like an alarm. But eventually, he grew to love travel.

My mother’s ideas on the consequences of travel weren’t edicts, and they didn’t have to be my fate. They were anxiety-driven beliefs that I had the choice to keep or discard. I began to see the power in decision-making: I could narrow Beau’s world, as my mother had done to mine, or give him — and, in the process, myself — the tools to expand it.

Freedom From Fear

I discovered a far-off dog park so large you can’t see its boundaries from the entrance, a refuge of rolling hills and woodsy trails buffeted on three sides by a bay. Although the drive took 45 minutes to an hour each way and entailed traversing city streets, tunnels, bridges and highways, I took Beau there weekly. There, fear wasn't around. Beau galloped with other dogs, as if he were a freed horse, splashing through the water and across grassy fields, rolling on his back, in the mud, gazing up at the sky with a wide tongue-dangling smile, panting with pure joy.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Driving the long way home one day, my hands on the steering wheel, I became aware, for the first time, of the absence of my fear. Glancing in the rearview mirror, I saw Beau curled up in the backseat, sleeping.

Love, not fear, can take us anywhere. What can you doggedly overcome today?

This post contains excerpts adapted from a previously-published essay in Salon

item.title: How Aparna Nancherla Learned to Live with Her Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

How Aparna Nancherla Learned to Live with Her Anxiety

The comedian reflects on anxiety, self-doubt, imposter syndrome, and the power of humor.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • In an interview, comedian Aparna Nancherla shares how anxiety has shaped her life.
  • Anxiety creates persistent challenges—yet the anxious mind can also be a powerful source of insight and humor.
  • Humor won't erase anxiety, she notes, but it can connect people through shared experience.
Aparna Nancherla
Source: "Anxiety Club" film

Since first watching the documentary "Anxiety Club," I have written several articles inspired by both the film itself and the amazing conversations it has sparked. Directed and produced by Wendy Lobel, the film offers an honest and compassionate look at anxiety, reminding viewers how common, complex, and deeply human the experience is.

I also had the opportunity to attend the film's launch event at New York's legendary Comedy Cellar, where many of the featured comedians took the stage to share their insights and perspectives on living with anxiety. The documentary examines how anxiety impacts people's lives, relationships, careers, and sense of self. As part of my ongoing series of interviews, I recently had the pleasure of speaking with comedian, writer, actor, and author Aparna Nancherla about her experiences living with anxiety.

"I Didn't Call It Anxiety for a Long Time"

"I always was an anxious person," Nancherla told me. "My mom always called me a worrier, but I didn't call it anxiety for a long time." As an adult, however, she was able to identify it as anxiety and became increasingly interested in understanding how it operated in her life, when it emerged, and how it influenced her thoughts and behaviors.

"My anxiety is on its own journey," she explained, noting that its manifestation continues to change over time. Like many people who live with chronic anxiety, she has found that managing it often involves paying attention to basic practices that are easy to dismiss, such as getting enough sleep, staying hydrated, and eating well. "They sound so simple," she said, "but they really do make a difference."

She acknowledges that these habits can be difficult to sustain in a fast-paced culture where productivity is often prioritized above health. Being more intentional about daily choices has improved her ability to regulate her nervous system. She also states that therapy, mindfulness, and somatic practices have helped her identify recurring patterns and better understand how her mind responds to stress.

During our conversation, Nancherla described what she called an "anxious brain" as an inability to take things at face value, constantly anticipating what might happen next and thinking about all the things that can go wrong. "[My brain] is always thinking ten steps ahead," she said, "and being very creative in imagining worst-case scenarios."

This tendency to scan, gather information, analyze possibilities, and search for potential threats is at the foundation of anxiety. From an evolutionary perspective, this vigilance is protective and necessary for survival. As Nancherla noted, it comes down to the basic question: "Is that a stick or a snake?"

Finding the Funny Side of Anxiety

For Nancherla, anxiety and comedy overlap in interesting ways. The observational qualities that often accompany anxiety, she noted, can also fuel humor. Noticing details, nuances, contradictions, and social dynamics can provide rich material to work with. Comedy can emerge from taking those insights and presenting them in exaggerated, unexpected, and illuminating ways.

Nancherla's path into comedy began in high school, where she discovered that she enjoyed making people laugh. "I didn't know I was funny," she recalled. "I would run cross-country and make little jokes and people would laugh." Later, after she'd begun to recognize her own sense of humor and the satisfaction that came from sharing laughter with others, she discovered stand-up comedy through open mics and was surprised by how much she enjoyed performing. "I liked to perform, which was unexpected."

But even though she enjoyed performing, it amplified her anxiety. She remembers intense stage fright, a racing heart, a tight throat, and, at times, feeling physically sick after performing. For Nancherla, comedy required learning how to manage anxiety onstage and off, which has been an ongoing practice.

Many people assume that stand-up comedy and social anxiety are mutually exclusive. Comedians who speak openly about their mental health are often asked how standing in front of a crowd and sharing deeply personal stories can coexist with their anxiety.

However, unlike a party or social gathering, where people must continuously monitor social cues and navigate unpredictable interactions, stand-up has a predictable formula, Nancherla said. "You talk and then you disappear—you don't owe them anything." The performer controls the material, the timing, and the duration is a pre-established amount of time.

She also described comedy as a tension many people experience: the desire to express oneself authentically while simultaneously seeking acceptance and validation from others. Sharing personal experiences with an audience can be an intensely vulnerable act, particularly when the material touches on insecurity, fear, or emotional pain.

Anxiety Under the Spotlight

Many of these themes found their way into her memoir, Unreliable Narrator. The book explores self-doubt, impostor syndrome, and the critical inner voice that can accompany success. Interestingly, she found that increased visibility often amplified these struggles. "The negative self-talk got worse as I got more traction and more exposure in my career."

Writing the memoir gave her an opportunity to examine these experiences on a deeper level. In our conversation, she reflected on the ways that stand-up can require compressing observations into bite-sized bits. It's also very structured, whereas a memoir allows for ambiguity. "The book can be messier—and stressful, because you can't control what other people think of it."

Writing honestly about her inner critic and exposing parts of herself that felt shameful or vulnerable was emotionally demanding. The experience was destabilizing at times yet ultimately rewarding. After publication, she found that distance helped her develop a better relationship with the work and gave her a sense of pride that was difficult to access while she was writing it. "I survived that," she said, looking back.

Contemporary culture often treats pauses as failures and periods of reduced productivity as evidence that nothing meaningful is happening. There is ongoing pressure to create, achieve, and move on to the next project. Many artists become accustomed to the question: "So, what are you working on next?"

"It's almost like you don't exist as a creator if you're not producing something all the time," she said.

Anxiety often pulls attention toward what might happen next, making it difficult to stay in the present. Nancherla indicated that by bringing together comedians who speak openly about their fears, coping strategies, and vulnerabilities, "Anxiety Club" humanizes the experience of living with anxiety. One of the most moving aspects of participating in the documentary for her was seeing how anxiety shows up in other comedians' lives and learning how they navigate it day by day. Ultimately, "Anxiety Club" reminds viewers that even our most persistent fears can become sources of insight, connection, and sometimes laughter.

item.title: Watching Sports Is Good for Your Well-Being
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Watching Sports Is Good for Your Well-Being

Emotional engagement in sports may shape well-being for all ages.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Watching sports helps foster social connections and generates great emotional experiences.
  • Both watching in real-life and on television can improve how you feel.
  • However, if you watch sports on television, don't sit till too much as that is not good for you.

The FIFA World Cup is in full swing, and around the world, millions of people are watching. For some, missing a game may seem inconceivable. Many have travelled to see the games live, whilst others may be watching on television.

There is plenty of media coverage full of people expressing their happiness when their teams are doing well and sadness when they are being outperformed. I don’t think anyone would argue that watching sports can generate strong emotions. However, some emotions may be linked to stress. Not knowing which team will win and hoping your team will come back when they are down a point or two can generate negative emotions. It is perfectly feasible to ask whether it is good for people to watch sports.

Benefits of watching sports

Whilst you may think that watching sport in person would be better for you than watching it on television or online, research suggests that both have a positive impact on the sports consumer. Watching sports can enhance well-being, primarily through fostering social connections and enriching emotional experiences. When visiting sporting events, you may chat to others and feel that you belong. It may also become a topic of conversation with others after the game itself, as many discuss events they have attended. However, the latter can also be true for watching televised sporting events.

Researchers have found that watching sports is associated with increased brain activity and structural volume in reward circuits—brain regions related to feelings of happiness or pleasure. Brain activity was larger in the reward circuit when watching a popular sport compared with a less popular one. This, in turn, was connected to daily sport-watching behaviours. The longer people watch sports daily, the greater the impact of watching on their well-being. Interestingly, the study showed evidence that brain structures may change due to daily sports watching. Such a change may result in people feeling greater well-being more readily.

Source: Courtesy of Vitaly Gariev/Pexels

The positive effect of watching sports is not age-restricted. An analysis of over 5000 older people in Japan (over 6 years) found that watching sports (both in real life and on screen) was associated with a reduced risk of worsening depressive symptoms. Furthermore, as in younger people, it was associated with enhanced social well-being—people were more likely to see more friends.

The social element to watching sports is undoubtedly a key reason why it makes people feel good; socialising has many benefits. For example, in residential care for older adults, taking part in fortnightly social activities can help reduce depression and anxiety as well as increase social identification with other people. If sporting events help with socialising, it is clearly positive.

Word of caution

Whilst watching sports can make people feel good, it is worth bearing in mind that if watched primarily via a screen, inactivity may result. This can explain why watching sports on media has been associated with a higher body mass index, as well as higher risks of developing hypertension and diabetes.

Enhancing the well-being of individuals is a universally sought-after objective; perhaps the world needs more large sporting events. People could even be encouraged to watch sports as a new public health initiative!

item.title: Psychopathy in Children: What Can Be Done?
item.description:
Psychopathy

Psychopathy in Children: What Can Be Done?

Early diagnosis, intervention, treatment, and how schools can help.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Early intervention can reduce aggression and impulsivity in children with psychopathic traits.
  • Intensive, individualized treatment programs lower antisocial behaviors in callous-unemotional youth.
  • Self-report diagnostic tools by youth align better with clinician assessments than caregiver reports.
  • Schools may overlook children with conduct disorders due to gaps in special education law coverage.

“Once a psychopath, always a psychopath” is an apt aphorism for what many have traditionally concluded about adults displaying very high levels of psychopathic traits. Lack of remorse or shame, no feelings of guilt, callous and unemotional acts, poor behavioral controls, manipulative scheming, cunning preying on others … all these are typical psychopathic traits that can endure in such people over their lifetimes.

Many researchers have documented the reality that the few treatment programs for them typically produce little, if any, change.1 But … what if there were interventions while still young? Is there any hope then?

Source: u fliigxc09 /Pixabay

Early age intervention

Preeminent psychopathy researcher, Dr. Robert D. Hare, noted in his popular work, Without Conscience, The Disturbing World of the Psychopaths Among Us, that perhaps by intervening at a very early age, it might be possible “to modify the behavioral patterns of ‘budding psychopaths’ by reducing aggression and impulsivity and by teaching them strategies for satisfying their needs in more prosocial ways.”2

Treatment programs and their effectiveness

In a summary of six “high-quality” studies of the efficacy of various treatment modalities for youth with high levels of psychopathic traits or callous-unemotional behavior, psychology researchers, Drs. Devon Polaschek and Jennifer Skeem, state, "The main conclusion that can be drawn from these studies is that children and adolescents with callous-unemotional features respond to prevention and intensive treatment with reduced antisocial behavior.”3 In particular, they noted the success of an intensive custodial treatment program with 45 programming weeks when compared to custodial treatment as usual.

Other studies Polaschek and Skeem analyzed looked at the use of multisystemic therapy ("MST"). This is a family-based program with intensive elements intended to minimize out-of-home placements. They showed limited effectiveness, but the researchers concluded that including more intensive, personalized approaches that targeted the children’s callous-unemotional features would increase the treatment’s benefits.

Diagnostic tools, their value and shortcomings

Intensive programs focusing on a child’s callous-unemotional behavior may be helpful, but what diagnostic tools are available to measure the degree to which a child evinces psychopathic traits?4 The most famous of these tools is the Psychopathy Checklist - Youth Version (“PCL:YV”). This measure of psychopathic traits was an adaptation of the Psychopathy Checklist - Revised (“PCL-R”), the gold standard 20-item test for psychopathy developed by Dr. Robert Hare that has been vetted in countless studies. The PCL:YV is also a 20-item instrument designed to measure the degree to which a juvenile exhibits 20 psychopathic traits.

It is administered through a semi-structured interview of the child conducted by a trained clinician plus a detailed historical document review. The other principal diagnostic tools are self-report measures that are completed by the child and the child’s caregiver. These tools include The Antisocial Process Screening Device (“APSD”), the Inventory of Callous – Unemotional Traits (“ICU”), the Child Psychopathy Scale (“CPS”), and the Youth Psychopathic Inventory (“YPI”). Each of these four tools are done through self-report and include separate youth and caregiver versions. These tests are designed primarily for early-to-late adolescence. The APSD is intended to be used for children as young as 9 years old.

A report in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology, authored by a team including noted psychopathy researcher Kent Kiehl, determined that “evidence is mounting that suggests that early, individualized interventions are effective in ameliorating the antisocial behavior of these youth.”5 Comparing use of the different diagnostic tools showed good diagnostic correlation between the self-reports completed by the youths themselves and results from the PCL:YV. The caregiver assessments, however, showed poor agreement, thereby urging caution in their diagnostic use. But while diagnostic tools exist that can help identify children with high degrees of psychopathic traits or callous-unemotionality, who does this testing, where, and how is it accessed?

The role of schools and needed improvements

Teachers and counselors at schools are front-line observers of children’s behavior every day and are often in the best position to sense the level of conduct disorder and emotional interactions among their students. A recent review of the assessment and treatment of youth in schools noted that many supports exist for students identified under special education law, but that those supports may be unavailable to students showing extreme conduct disorder.6 The law states that it does not apply to students who are “socially maladjusted,” unless there is also an emotional disturbance. Some children showing conduct disorders, aggressive behavior, and callous-unemotional traits may fall through the cracks.

Schools must be mindful that they have an obligation to evaluate and diagnose these children as well. If the results of the diagnostic tools suggest high levels of psychopathic traits, targeted intervention and supports must be implemented as soon as possible. The answer is not discipline, suspension or expulsion. Intensive supports and therapeutic interventions are essential. Failure to do this may save money in the short term, but that failure may cause extreme human and societal suffering if a child is not prevented from becoming a full-blown psychopath.

item.title: Raising Emotionally Healthy Kids in the Digital Age
item.description:
Child Development

Raising Emotionally Healthy Kids in the Digital Age

An interview with veteran educators Steven Shapiro and Nancy Shapiro Rapport

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Parents are having to compete with social media influencers and AI companions for kids’ attention.
  • Traditional community reinforcement of family values is facing powerful competition from online influences.
  • Building a strong, intentional family culture can help kids resist corrosive digital pressures.
  • Better family conversations and greater parent-child trust can make parents the go-to resource for guidance.

Recent study findings reflect a concern brewing in the hearts and minds of parents and educators: Are we adequately preparing students for this increasingly digital age? For example:

  • Pew Research Center revealed that nearly half of U.S. teens now believe that social media has a mostly negative effect on people their age; this is a sharp increase from the 32 percent who felt this way in 2022 (Faverio, Anderson, & Park, 2025).
  • Common Sense Media found that one in three children are already using AI for social interaction and emotional support (Robb & Mann, 2025).
  • The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)’s National Center for Health Statistics reported that teens spending four or more hours daily on screens are more than twice as likely to experience anxiety and depression (Zablotsky, Arockiaraj, Haile, & Ng, 2024).
Source: Rajesh Rajput / Unsplash

Journal papers and news headlines regularly bring us new findings along these lines. The world is rapidly changing, so homes and schools need to keep up. But how?

Amid this unprecedented terrain, veteran educators Steven Shapiro and Nancy Shapiro Rapport cofounded Our Family Culture to help parents raise emotionally healthy kids. Their angle on this goal is unique: building intentional family cultures. Intrigued by this approach’s potential, I joined their Board of Advisors and asked them about how intentional family cultures can help children and teens withstand today’s (and tomorrow’s) digital forces. The sibling duo’s answers follow each interview question below.

Jenny Rankin (JR): How has technology, including AI, increased the challenges of parenting?

Steven Shapiro (SS) and Nancy Shapiro Rapport (NSR): If you feel like parenting is harder in the digital age, you’re not imagining it. Modern parents are navigating unprecedented competition for their children’s attention, hearts, and minds.

Historically, parents could count on their surrounding community to reinforce the values and beliefs they taught at home. Neighbors, extended family, and local institutions largely reiterated those lessons. Now, a fractured and increasingly contentious world has eroded, and at times negated, that reinforcement.

Instead of community support, parents now compete with a litany of social media influencers vying for their kids’ attention. The range of influencers shaping our children’s worldview is staggering, and the impact can be devastating. Many parents are losing their kids to voices promoting unhealthy values and actions, from the misogynist “manosphere” to pro-eating-disorder influencers.

With the rapid rise of AI companions and bots, children are also subject to influence from non-human “relationships.” The most tragic examples involve young people who have taken their own lives at the encouragement of an AI chatbot. Clearly, it is a very challenging time to be a parent.

JR: How can parents protect their kids from these influences?

SS and NSR: Jonathan Haidt, in The Anxious Generation, makes a compelling case for delaying children’s access to social media. We concur.

But responsible parenting in the digital age requires something more: the intentional practice of raising children grounded enough to resist negative messaging from social media influencers and AI companions. That means taking deliberate action to cultivate deeply rooted values at home, creating a clear family culture that protects children from the seductive and often corrosive influences they will inevitably encounter online.

People easily recognize the importance of team culture in sports and organizational culture at work. However, many parents overlook the most important culture of all: their family culture.

JR: How does one build a strong family culture?

SS & NSR: There are three steps:

1. Identify Your Core Values. Building a strong family culture begins with defining the values you most want your children to internalize. There is no single correct set; they should flow naturally from your own core beliefs. Some families center on kindness, creativity, and wonder. Others emphasize integrity, hard work, and resilience. What matters is that parents can clearly articulate the kind of kids they hope to raise, and that in two-parent households, both partners are aligned.

2. Translate Values Into Behavior-Based Language. Values alone are too abstract to teach. Parents should, instead, focus on actionable language. In his book Culture by Design, David Friedman calls this the Fundamentals System: turning values into concrete, behavior-based phrases. “Do the right thing” is more teachable than “integrity.” “Bounce back” is more actionable than “resilience.” This shared language becomes a shorthand families can use every day.

3. Practice Consistently. Culture isn’t built in a single conversation. It emerges from many small, repeated interactions. The practical approach is to choose one Fundamental each week and give it a small amount of attention daily: a question at dinner, a personal story, a short video, a moment of reflection. Cycle through your Family Fundamentals, then start again. Over time, they stop being words and become the essence of who your family is: “We are the Shapiros. We show up for others.”

JR: What can parents realistically expect from this kind of intentional effort?

SS & NSR: The most immediate shift families notice is in the quality of everyday conversations. When a family shares a common language around values, difficult moments become opportunities to talk about principles rather than problems. A child who pushes back, siblings in conflict, a parenting partner who sees things differently: all of these become chances to ask, “What does our family believe here?” rather than simply reacting.

Beyond that, the work strengthens something that is often underestimated: the parent-child relationship itself. That trusted connection makes parents the first call, not the last resort, when children encounter the darker corners of the digital world. And in an era when the outside world has never been more aggressive about shaping who your children will become, that connection is everything.
