item.title: The Shift We Need: Why a Hybrid Caring Economy Starts Inside
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Shift We Need: Why a Hybrid Caring Economy Starts Inside

The interplay of aspirations and algorithms

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • AI mirrors and amplifies the values embedded by its human creators and users.
  • Prosocial AI requires examining values before coding, not just fixing biased data later.
  • Mindset, not just technology, forms the true infrastructure of a caring economy.
The transition toward a caring economy and prosocial AI starts inside human attention.
Source: AI-Generated / ChatGPT. 2026

The future of artificial intelligence will be shaped by the mindset with which we build, buy, regulate, and use technology. We cannot expect the technology of tomorrow to be better than the humans of today, us.

For decades, modern economies have trained the human mind to focus on what can be counted quickly: quarterly returns, productivity metrics, rankings, clicks, speed, scale, and growth. These indicators help coordinate complex systems. Yet when they become the dominant definition of value, they reshape our attention. People become outputs.

Let’s be clear: trust and dignity are not pleasant additions to “real” economy; they are factors on which it depends. Competitiveness is not a numerical game show, because meaningful success goes beyond bottom-line business. Especially in a hybrid context, it matters to remember that.

A common-good economy sits at the heart of prosocial AI because both begin with a wider idea of value. A caring economy asks that human life be valued beyond immediate material output. Prosocial AI refers to AI systems that are deliberately tailored, trained, tested, and targeted to bring out the best in and for people and the planet. Together, they invite the shift from narrow return-on-value metrics to a rich hybrid return-on-values matrix. Change is overdue.

When Metrics Shape Mindsets

Every society teaches people what to notice. In a short-term economy, we learn to notice what moves numbers fast. The leader asks, “How much did we gain?” before asking, “What did we strengthen?” The institution asks, “How efficient is this?” before asking, “Who became more capable?” The platform asks, “What keeps attention?” before asking, “What deserves attention?”

Over time, questions become habits. Habits become incentives. Incentives become institutions. Institutions become culture, and culture confirms habits. Rather than measuring what we treasure, we begin to treasure what we can easily measure.

The problem becomes apparent in our attitude to care. Raising children, supporting elders, listening to distress, helping colleagues, mentoring young people, preventing harm, and maintaining trust are foundational forms of value creation. They make everything else possible. Yet they rarely appear on a balance sheet.

The International Labour Organization estimated that 708 million women worldwide were outside the labor force in 2023 because of unpaid care responsibilities. The World Inequality Report 2026 shows that women work longer hours than men once unpaid domestic and care work is included, while receiving only about one-third of total labor income.

We have built systems that depend on care while teaching ourselves to undervalue it.

AI Amplifies the Values We Pursue

AI enters this landscape as a mirror and a multiplier. It does not arrive with discernment and is bare of compassion. It learns human patterns, optimizes goals, predicts behavior, and scales instructions. As long as it is designed, delivered, and deployed with a mindset of short-term material value maximization, it will pursue that mindset with ever greater speed and reach. Is that success?

A company that treats people mainly as cost centers may use AI to monitor, rank, and replace. A school system obsessed with standardized performance may use AI to narrow learning. The danger goes beyond biased data or faulty algorithms. The deeper danger is impoverished purpose.

This is where prosocial AI can serve as a mindset upgrade with systemic benefit. It asks builders and users to examine their personal values before these are tacitly embedded in code, before datasets are selected, before dashboards are designed. It begins before the business model is locked into a prison of value fixation that forgoes the values that matter. Let's take a step back and face our own humanity before we invest billions in amplifying it online.

The scope of the hybrid era depends on intimate value deliberation far more than it does on technical features.

Beyond Short-Term Material Value

A society that measures mainly short-term material indicators will build AI for speed, scale, prediction, persuasion, substitution, and control. A society that values human flourishing will build AI for agency, dignity, learning, care, social connection, prevention, and planetary responsibility.

Economic performance matters. People need income, housing, food, infrastructure, medicine, education, and security. Yet material indicators become dangerous when they detach from the human and ecological conditions that make life worth living. A rising productivity curve can coexist with exhausted workers. A booming platform can deepen anxiety. A profitable product can weaken attention. A smart system can reduce friction while increasing dependence.

Is that a world we want to live in? Is it a place that we will be proud to leave behind for the next generation to inherit? That is why the UNDP Human Development Report 2025 matters for the AI age. It frames AI as a choice about human development, not simply a technological capability. The WHO Commission on Social Connection similarly reminds us that connection is central to health. These perspectives widen the lens, and they zoom in on one central question: What kind of human does AI encourage us to become?

Care as Economic Intelligence

Care is often misread as emotional generosity. It is also a form of intelligence. To care well is to perceive context. It requires attention, timing, restraint, memory, empathy, judgment, and imagination. A caregiver reads incomplete signals. A teacher senses when a student is present in body and absent in spirit. A nurse notices the difference between a symptom and a fear. A good manager recognizes when high performance masks exhaustion. This intelligence is relational, embodied, and contextual. It cannot be fully captured in a metric. It can, however, be supported or damaged by the systems around it.

Prosocial AI can serve to support humans imbued with caring intelligence. It can reduce administrative load, detect patterns early, widen access to knowledge, translate complexity, and help people make wiser choices. It can help institutions see where stress accumulates, where exclusion repeats, where support is missing, and where prevention would be wiser than repair.

Yet AI becomes prosocial only when guided by a mature human mindset. The same dashboard that reveals burnout can be used to blame workers. The same prediction model that identifies need can be used to deny services. The same personalization engine that supports learning can be used to manipulate desire.

Technology magnifies intention. That is why mindset is infrastructure.

The A-Frame Mindset

The transition toward a caring economy and prosocial AI starts inside human attention. The A-Frame mindset offers four practical entry points.

  1. Awareness means seeing the values already shaping our choices. Ask what your metrics reward, what they ignore, and how they influence behavior.
  2. Appreciation means recognizing forms of value that are easy to overlook. Care is intelligence. Relationships are infrastructure. Attention is finite. Human agency must be cultivated.
  3. Acceptance means facing the limits of short-term indicators. Numbers can guide decisions, yet they cannot carry the full meaning of a life, a community, or a planet. AI can process patterns; it cannot replace conscience, responsibility, or lived wisdom.
  4. Accountability means aligning tools with values. Ask who benefits, who carries the burden, who can challenge the outcome, and what long-term effects are being created.

The next frontier is situated inside. We need to retrain our individual and collective attention, measure what matters, and protect what must first be noticed before it can be valued and amplified.

item.title: Why Does Marriage Seem to Benefit Men More Than Women?
item.description:
Marriage

Why Does Marriage Seem to Benefit Men More Than Women?

What gender socialization has to do with health, happiness, and marriage.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Gender socialization shapes how men and women experience the benefits of marriage.
  • Marriage is associated with larger health and well-being benefits for men than for women.
  • Men often have fewer emotional support networks outside their romantic relationships.
Source: Image by Julia Malcher from Pixabay

This week, my partner scheduled two medical appointments in the same week. While I’m sure this felt a bit overwhelming for him, I couldn’t help feeling relieved that my months of reminders finally worked.

“Thanks for reminding me,” he said as he headed out the door for an appointment I had been encouraging him to make for quite some time. Half-jokingly, I found myself thinking: What would he do without me?

My question was asked in humor. But it also points to something I notice often in relationships—not just wives reminding husbands to schedule dentist appointments or medical visits, but a broader pattern in which one partner becomes the organizer, planner, and emotional manager of the relationship’s day-to-day functioning.

This dynamic raises a larger question researchers have been exploring for decades: why do men often appear to benefit more from marriage than women?

Gender socialization plays a part

For decades, researchers have noticed a consistent pattern: Marriage appears to provide greater health and psychological benefits for men than it does for women. At first glance, that conclusion may seem surprising—or even unfair. After all, both partners share the same relationship, so why would one partner benefit more?

The answer has less to do with marriage itself and more to do with the ways that many men and women are socialized to build relationships.

Some research finds that married men, on average, experience lower rates of depression and anxiety, reduced loneliness, better physical health, and even longer life expectancy compared to men who are unmarried1. A recent study from the University of Toronto similarly found that marital status was strongly associated with healthier aging outcomes among men, highlighting the long-term protective effects that marriage can have on men's well-being2. In short, the data suggests that men often see greater gains in key areas such as health, longevity, and financial well-being.

Importantly, these findings describe averages and associations—not universal outcomes. But the topic has become a meaningful point of discussion in social and health psychology—as well as a frequent punchline in everyday conversations about relationships.

Marriage and men’s psychological well-being

Across studies, married men tend to report lower levels of psychological distress—fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety, and greater emotional support and reduced isolation—compared to unmarried men. Marriage is also associated with more health-promoting behaviors in men, including increased preventive healthcare use, more regular medical appointments, and healthier lifestyle choices, which might be why research finds that married men also tend to show lower mortality rates than unmarried men1-3,5. In many cases, their partners play an active role in encouraging or facilitating these behaviors.

Marriage may provide men with something they don't receive elsewhere

One explanation for marriage "benefiting" men more is that, for many men, a spouse becomes their primary—and sometimes only—source of emotional support. Although this is not true for everyone, many men are socialized to limit emotional vulnerability in friendships and family relationships4. As a result, emotional expression may become concentrated within the romantic partnership.

Women, by contrast, are more often socialized to maintain emotionally rich networks outside their romantic relationships4. Friendships, family ties, and community connections can provide additional sources of support, meaning that the emotional benefits of connection are more distributed rather than centered in one relationship.

In this sense, marriage may not necessarily provide women with “less,” but may instead reflect how men are socialized to rely on romantic partners as their primary source of emotional support.4,5 When one partner is expected to provide most of the emotional support, relationship management, and caregiving, the costs and benefits of marriage may not be distributed equally.

Everyone benefits when emotional support is shared in a relationship

At the same time, scholars caution against overly simplistic interpretations. While many studies find larger average benefits for men, these patterns vary depending on the outcomes measured and how relationship quality is defined.³ Furthermore, some suggest that what appears to be a "marriage benefit" may actually reflect differences in how men and women are taught to seek support, express emotion, and care for one another.

Fortunately, these patterns are changing. Younger generations of men are increasingly developing emotionally intimate friendships, seeking therapy and other ways to deeper self-awareness, and expanding their support networks beyond their romantic partner. Couples are also becoming more intentional about sharing emotional labor and caregiving responsibilities.

Therefore, the question may not be whether marriage benefits men more than women, but what conditions create that appearance.

item.title: Online Gambling and the Losses It Brings
item.description:
Internet Addiction

Online Gambling and the Losses It Brings

The ability to place a bet—any time and any place—courts ruin for some people.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • A culture of instant gratification propels online gambling.
  • Young men have several risk factors for developing a gambling addiction.
  • Senior citizens are gambling online in steadily increasing ways.
  • Two fallacies often govern the way gamblers think.

We live in a culture that supercharges our wants and desires. We operate under a constant barrage of advertisements and enticements. Most of us are focused on what those pitched products or experiences promise us. Give us our joy, success, and pleasure. We happily concede to our flights of fancy instead of thinking about the likely disappointing or negative consequences.

The growth of online betting

Those ads and enticements feed an ever-growing hunger for instant gratification. This is becoming apparent with the exponential growth of online betting. A person can place an online bet at any time and from any place on an election outcome, a military action, or when a favorite animal at the zoo will give birth.

Sports betting is the easiest and most common form of online betting. It is becoming impossible to escape online sports betting. Whether watching on television or streaming, the odds for a match or game are constantly being shown. In major sporting events such as the Stanley Cup Hockey finals and the NBA finals, spectators were exposed to gambling marketing every 20 seconds.

Every shot, every point, every period score, and final score is an opportunity to place a bet.

Sports Illustrated has gone so far as to rank the top six online sports betting programs. Never mind discussing the sports themselves; SI now discusses betting on the sports.

Easy access to sports betting is creating a world of pain for many people. People no longer need to seek betting opportunities; they can find all sorts of opportunities on their phones. For young people who have grown up with their phones glued to their hands, the temptations may be too hard to ignore.

Risk factors for developing a gambling addiction include being male, younger in age, having a family history of gambling problems, certain personality traits, and co-occurring mental health disorders. The phone has never been more dangerous.

Older people are also beginning to participate in online gambling to very dangerous effect. Many seniors are now regular users of online gambling platforms that are available at every hour. People who have never gambled to a dangerous effect in the past are losing their retirements, spouses, and well-being.

Twin fallacies driving online betting

As players place more bets at higher amounts, they become victims of the sunk cost fallacy. The fallacy: I have already spent or lost so much money that I am willing to continue to invest and invest more heavily rather than re-evaluate my circumstances and change my behavior.

With a credit card conveniently stored on their phones, many using online betting apps may find themselves gambling more liberally than they would have. Senior citizens may have a very robust line of credit that can be decimated quickly. When people recognize the sunk cost fallacy and try to cut down on or quit these gambling platforms, they are often lured back with enticing offers. There are always workarounds for whatever self-imposed deposit, wager, or time limits a person may put on their account.

With gambling available on phones, it is very easy for seniors to hide in plain sight, hunched over their phone right next to younger people doing the same thing.

Winning will make some vulnerable to the aptly named gambler’s fallacy, the belief that past events influence future probabilities in independent events, such as thinking that after several losses, a win is due. It does not pertain to the belief that past performance guarantees future results. Combine this with the sunk cost fallacy, and the results can be devastating. In suffering significant losses from gambling, most people will feel deep shame. This may be especially true for people who always see themselves as hard-working and saving responsibly for their retirement. This shame may bring isolation and loneliness. Hiding losses from family members, confronting economic insecurity, and believing yourself to have ruined not only your future but your family’s is devastating.

Addictions in their myriad forms can spring from and reinforce loneliness and social isolation. Whether it is a younger person feeling as if he is already behind in his life or a senior whose identity and life have been altered by retirement, loss of a spouse, or adult children who are busy with their own lives, gambling promises excitement and the possibility of a payout. The payout may be small at first, but the jolt of joy accompanying it isn’t. For those who feel lonely, isolated, or simply flat in much of their daily life, that jolt is seductive.

Don’t mistake that jolt for joy. That jolt may be the harbinger of shame.

item.title: How Happiness Leads to Heart Health
item.description:
Health

How Happiness Leads to Heart Health

Research shows older adults in happy relationships experience the most benefit.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Positive co-experiences lower cortisol levels more than positive emotions experienced alone.
  • Shared joyful moments measurably reduce stress at a biological level.
  • Experiencing joy or contentment reduces stress, especially in happy relationships.
  • The health benefits of shared happiness are more pronounced in older adults.

Recent field research is authenticating the age-old association people make between the psychological (feelings) and the biological (the heart). Studies now confirm that happy moods create measurable physiological changes.

The 2026 World Happiness Report (WHR) notes that its quarter-century of research continues to support a finding in psychology that longevity and immunity are boosted not by the absence of negative emotions but by the presence of positive emotions. This is true across wide demographics and in all relationships, but is particularly pronounced among older adults. The health benefits of happy moods are boosted when positive feelings are shared with others and enhanced even more when the mood is shared between people who feel good about the relationship.

Field and Lab Studies Align

Tomiko Yoneda, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Davis, was the lead author of a 2024 study investigating co-experienced positive emotions in couples’ daily lives. From 2012 to 2018, Yoneda and her team measured saliva cortisol levels concurrent with the self-reported emotional states of 321 older adult couples aged 56–89 years multiple times a day for a week in three studies in Canada and Germany. She notes that the study’s field findings concur with previous laboratory studies that show a relationship between happiness, longevity, resilience, and a stronger immune response due to reduced long-term cortisol exposure, which supports better overall health.

What Love Has to Do With It

Results show that when relationship partners are together, both partners report positive emotions higher than their baseline individual moods 38 percent of the time. When their partner reported higher positive emotions than usual, study participants produced less of the stress hormone cortisol. This effect was even stronger than when each individual reported their independent positive emotions. It was also stronger for the people who reported being happier in their relationship.

The research finds that the benefits of co-experienced positive emotions extend beyond the immediate moment they are felt, lowering cortisol secretion in the moment and at subsequent measurements. Yoneda explains that having a happy intimate partner not only lifts the other partner’s mood but also helps both manage stress, especially for older adults.

The Science of Emotional Well-Being

Experiencing shared happiness, relaxation, genuine joy, or contentment triggers the release of brain neurotransmitters, including dopamine, serotonin, and endorphins. These chemical messengers make us feel good, reduce inflammation, strengthen immune function, and protect cardiovascular systems.

Daily feelings affect cortisol production, which spikes with acute stress. Negative emotions are linked to higher cortisol levels, and chronically elevated cortisol can lead to poorer overall health.

Yoshida notes that with aging, the links between emotions and cortisol may be more pronounced. Older adults tend to have stronger physiological responses to stress, and their bodies are less able to slow down their cortisol production. Sharing a happy moment can buffer cortisol production, contributing to healthier aging.

Yoneda said, “These research results are consistent with a psychological theory that suggests positive emotions increase our ability to act more fluidly in the moment. These experiences can create a positive feedback loop that enhances this ability over time.”

item.title: How Undergrieving Keeps You Stuck
item.description:
Grief

How Undergrieving Keeps You Stuck

Why you need to acknowledge and process the loss before you plan your future.

Posted July 1, 2026

Source: fizkes/Shutterstock

You have been making plans. You have been setting goals. You have been telling yourself that the future is bright, that the past is behind you, that forward is the only direction worth traveling.

And yet, things don’t work out the way you planned.

The promotions you chase feel hollow when they come. The relationships you enter collapse for reasons you cannot name. The energy you pour into work, into children, into the nonstop busyness of life, does not seem either enough or fitting. As if there is a ceiling you cannot break through, no matter how hard you try. It makes you tired. You feel stuck and do not find an explanation why.

It’s very possible that the pain that holds you back arrived long ago and is still unrecognized and unnamed.

Undergrieving or disenfranchised grief

Kenneth Doka tells the story of Marcus. (2) His parents had divorced, and at twelve years old he began to act out at school. His mother was bewildered: "He sees his dad whenever he wants, it's not like he is dead. There is no reason for him to behave like that!"

However, divorce, separation, the death of a relationship—all these losses are very real. They are losses of connection, of continuity, of the world as it was. But in today’s world, it seems, we only get the right to grieve about a close family member who has passed away, and it is the only permissible significant loss.

Doka reminds us that serious mourning can occur even when the object of loss remains physically alive. Marcus was acting out in the attempt to grieve a future that would never arrive. A family that would never reform. A father who would never come home at night. His grief was not recognized because the death had not occurred.

Yes, Marcus was just 12, but we in our 30s, 40s, and 50s also tend to regress to a psychologically much younger age during stressful events due to life shifts. We are lost, we want help, we want to get a break from all that, just like children.

Take another example (3). During the onset of the COVID pandemic, there was a couple whose fertility treatment was delayed and ended without success. Formally, nobody died, but the experience of not having the long-desired pregnancy made the couple feel isolated and induced powerlessness.

Infertility-related grief got disenfranchised: it did not attract increased social support or usual comforting rituals which would come following a death of a relative. The couple got stuck in the loop of the stages of grief: denial, anger, bargaining, sadness—being unable to complete the work of grief, as the loss remained unformulated and therefore unacknowledged.

Moreover, the "supportive" attempts to minimize the pain with comments like "you can always try again" or "adopt" made the processing of the loss even harder, amplifying the isolation.

We are not taught to formulate things as a loss. We are not conditioned to see something important that we lose, especially lose suddenly and unexpectedly—as worthy of grieving and processing, before we move on.

You might be doing the same now. Maybe you have buried something. Perhaps not a death, perhaps a divorce, a layoff, a betrayal, a dream that crumbled in your hands, a relationship that ended without closure. You told yourself to get over it. You convinced yourself that strong people move on. You told yourself that the past is the past. You supported yourself with the words that you can try again.

And now you are stuck.

Underappreciation of grief and loss processing

Grief is the most underappreciated emotional process, because it’s painful, so people tend to shun it and label it “a waste of time”. You might think: why spend time grieving and be sad when I can spend it building a brighter future? You tell yourself: “I will not look into the loss, I’ll just find other ways. Besides, if I build the future I dream of, the past won’t matter any longer.”

However, the ungrieved things may be the reason why things in your present don't work out and you can’t build the future you desire.

Teleporting into the future, brushing past that you’ve lost something or someone significant, doesn't work—not just psychologically, but also biologically. Because your brain forms attachments.

John Bowlby, the psychiatrist who spent a lifetime studying how we bond and what happens when those bonds are broken, called this the attachment system (1). When you form a deep attachment to someone or something, your brain encodes that relationship at a fundamental level. It becomes part of your internal wiring. And when that attachment is severed, something in you remains tethered to what is gone.

The ghost of the past event does not care about your five-year plan. It does not respond to affirmations. And the ghost does not respect your schedule.

It waits for you to notice it.
It pulls you back.
It drains your energy.

Do you know why you are exhausted? Because you run. And you know why you run? Because you are not sure how to process the past.

Jumping into the future becomes a form of escapism. When you have been laid off, and you devote yourself undivided to your children, even though it wasn’t required to such an extent, or when you have been divorced, and you immediately pour all your energy into work, without processing what has been taken from you—these are compensations. They are attempts to fill the void with noise, with motion, and with purpose.

Though they might temporarily serve as pain alleviation, they are not a full-scale, long-term solution. That’s why therapy in transitory times focuses so much on processing loss, instead of helping you be uber-productive or push you forward.

Why grief is the opposite of depression

Sigmund Freud understood this distinction more than a century ago. In his foundational essay “Mourning and Melancholia”, he drew a line between two responses to loss (4). Mourning, what we would call healthy grieving, is a process of slowly withdrawing emotional energy from what is lost and eventually reinvesting it in life. It is painful, but it is natural. As it runs its course, the person emerges—changed but whole.

Melancholia, what we would call depression, is different. In melancholia, the person cannot let go. The attachment is not released. Instead, the lost person or thing becomes internalized, absorbed into the self, and the anger and longing that should have been directed outward are turned inward. The mourner attacks himself. He or she becomes stuck.

Grieving is the opposite of depression. By acknowledging, processing, and grieving the loss, you create a connection between the past, the present, and the future.

Depression, as many studies suggest, is when you are unable to let go of something and you long for it. Your energy is being taken by staying with it without being able to part from it. You are suspended—not moving forward, not fully present, just stuck, with one hand still reaching for what is already gone. (Read my article on depression)

That is why grief work matters so much. That is why Doka insists that validation and creative interventions are essential. Because when grief is disenfranchised: hidden, dismissed, or minimized, it does not disappear, but curdles and rots, like old milk. It becomes something else: depression, anger, numbness, chronic fatigue, or that vague sense of being off that you cannot quite name.

Conclusion

An unrecognized, dismissed loss does not help you sprint forward. Instead, it severs your link with the past and creates a self-illusion in which you, family, and society might behave as if you have not lost anything significant. "You are still young", "There are so many things ahead of you" - as supportive as these things might sound, if they land on an unprocessed loss, they leave you tired, angry, disengaged from not being able to acknowledge and process what you have lost.

Different societies have different grieving rules and norms that specify who, when, where, and how people should grieve. Therapy is also instrumental in processing grief. It is not the essence of this article to codify grief in customs or cultural policies. It is to codify that if you've tried everything and are still tired, and your plans for the future don't work out, perhaps your past and your loss need attention. It needs to be identified, acknowledged, processed - in as much time as you need for it, so that you reclaim a legitimate right to grieve. And then your way forward will begin.

item.title: Why Leaving Home Doesn't Always Mean Moving On
item.description:
Identity

Why Leaving Home Doesn't Always Mean Moving On

How we get cognitively stuck in places we have left behind.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Sometimes we miss a place because it holds part of our identity.
  • Leaving a place does not always mean we have cognitively left it.
  • Sometimes we grieve places because they have become part of who we are.
  • Healing often begins by accepting loss rather than reclaiming the past.

A woman, "Mrs Fraught", sent the following email below to Annabel Rivkin and Emilie McMeekan, who write the column ‘The Midults’ in The Telegraph (UK):

My parents-in-law are downsizing, and my husband is so upset about it that he wants to buy the family house in Suffolk where he grew up. The problem is we have always lived and worked in London; the children are at great schools and happy; our friends are fab and mostly local; and we can in no way afford to take on another mortgage. It makes no sense. As lovely as the house and village are, they are for another family with another life. They have had a couple of offers, but he can talk about little else apart from moving home. We are arguing all the time and I’m at a loss about how to handle this.

At first glance, the issue seems straightforward; however, it is far more complicated. The writer's husband is about to lose a place he has continued to revisit psychologically, and perhaps physically, over the years; a place he returns to in order to reconnect with cherished memories.

Mrs Fraught, by contrast, appears ready to let the house go. She does not seem to have the same cognitive attachment to it. Given their financial position, their children’s schools, their social life in London, and the practical demands of work and commuting, it seems unreasonable to her to reorganise their present life around a house that belongs, emotionally at least, to her husband's past.

What her husband was experiencing was described by the columnists as "extreme nostalgia’. In their published response, they explained:

… [It] takes hold and makes us feel safe – sepia-ing out all rational thought and leaving us with a tinted view of what home and happiness mean. The world seems a fragile and febrile place right now; if only we could all go back to a better time and a better place where things were simpler. It’s not particularly surprising that your husband has latched on to the security of his childhood in Suffolk; imagine for a minute being 10 and on a BMX bike, buying Refreshers in the village shop and the day unfolding with no expectations or pressure.

Viewed through the lens of cognitive immobility, Mrs Fraught's husband appears to be experiencing more than nostalgia. He is not simply cognitively attached to that place; he may have been living with the psychological conditions associated with cognitive immobility for years.

When Losing a Place Feels Like Losing Yourself

Those in the first stage of cognitive immobility — awareness and separation — become aware of the longing and loss that follow leaving a place, thing or relationship. As they experience this separation, they may try to cognitively re-experience what that place or relationship once provided or physically return in search of solace (Olumba, 2023). The second stage, retrieval, occurs, as I noted in Transforming Society, when:

… individuals attempt to resolve the issue of being entrapped in a location or life experience by making efforts to retrieve the lost item, person or home. If they cannot do so by physically travelling there or in person, they mentally re-experience the incidents by recognising and recreating memories, a process which can cause discomfort. When the unconscious remembering sets in, the mental journey becomes stressful.

In this man's case, it might have been possible that returning to his childhood home over the years has helped ease his sense of loss and longing while preserving his emotional connection to it.

Now that the family home is about to be sold, the prospect of losing this space of comfort and refuge may have triggered his insistence that he buy it to hold onto it. This can be understood as the retrieval stage. People who enter this stage often require support. Without it, the distress can intensify and, as I have explained elsewhere, it could lead to anger, despair, a sense of loss, depression and even psychosis in the affected individual.

This stage of cognitive immobility resembles mourning, as it is marked by deep sadness, loss, and pain when present circumstances trigger memories of a lost place or former life experience (Olumba, 2023, p. 781; 2024; Kernberg, 2010).

It is therefore understandable why the letter-writer's husband would resist the sale of the house. Selling it would mean more than losing a family property; it could intensify his cognitive immobility and leave him with one of its defining features: a disrupted sense of identity and home (Olumba, 2024). If the place that has anchored his memories disappears, nowhere may truly feel like home again. He may have what I call a homeless mind.

Moving Forward: From Retrieval to Stabilisation

Annabel Rivkin and Emilie McMeekan were right when they observed that ‘Right now, he is flooded with feelings of vulnerability and rootlessness’. They advised Mrs Fraught:

It may be healthy for him to get involved with the move. That way it’s not happening to someone else; he doesn’t allow himself to be a child in the face of his parents’ move, and feel like an abandoned child when it’s gone, but rather get in there and help. He needs to be part of their journey now, helping tuck them in to their new space.

I believe this is sound advice because what this man needs now is to move towards the third stage of cognitive immobility, which consists of 'deliberate efforts to retain values and seek goals that will alleviate the loss'.

By becoming involved in his parents’ move and the sale of the family home, 'Mr Fraught' may begin to retain the values associated with that place rather than trying to hold on to the place itself. The process is unlikely to be easy. It may stir difficult emotions and painful memories. Yet actively participating in this transition could also help him gradually regain psychological stability and control. In other words, it might help him move into the third stage: stabilisation.

Many people struggle with a similar experience to that faced by this couple. Understanding why we feel so attached to certain places as well as recognising when those attachments begin to trap us psychologically is often the first step towards seeking support and finding a healthier way forward.
